content: The 2017 World Health Organization (WHO) guideline on preventive chemotherapy for controlling soil-transmitted helminth infections in at-risk populations provides evidence-based recommendations for reducing the burden of these infections. Soil-transmitted helminths, including roundworms, whipworms, and hookworms, are parasitic worms that cause significant morbidity, particularly in children, adolescents, and women of reproductive age. The guideline emphasizes the use of preventive chemotherapy, such as annual or biannual administration of single-dose albendazole (400 mg) or mebendazole (500 mg), as a public health intervention in endemic areas. The document outlines the methodology used to develop the recommendations, including systematic reviews of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and the application of the GRADE framework to assess the quality of evidence. The recommendations are intended for policymakers, healthcare providers, and program managers involved in designing and implementing helminth control programs. The guideline also addresses ethical and equity considerations, as well as the cost and feasibility of delivering deworming interventions. The guideline highlights the importance of targeting specific at-risk groups, such as preschool and school-age children, adolescent girls, and pregnant women, including those co-infected with HIV. It provides detailed evidence on the safety and efficacy of deworming medicines, the burden of disease caused by soil-transmitted helminths, and the impact of these infections on human health. The recommendations are supported by data on the benefits of reducing worm burden, improving nutritional outcomes, and enhancing overall public health. WHO acknowledges the contributions of various experts, technical groups, and organizations in the development of this guideline. Financial support for the work was provided by the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, among others.
